sections.html:
• Name: Malawa shrimp
  • Scientific name: Caridina pareparensis, Caridina parvidentata
  • Tank size (optimal): 20–40 litres
  • Breeding: easy
  • Optimal KH: 1–10
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour form: semi-transparent with many types of coloration (reddish, rusty, brownish, bluish, dark, etc.)

Malawa shrimp are very hardy and can be recommended for beginners. They do not interbreed with other dwarf shrimp species, so they can be kept in a community tank. They are a possible alternative to Ghost shrimp for keeping with small fish, shrimp and snails without risk of aggression. They have a semi-transparent body, which makes them a good replacement for Amano shrimp in aquascaping, as they do not distract from the scenery while cleaning and adding a little movement.

Their bodies are covered with tiny dots in reddish, rusty, brownish, bluish and dark colours, with many pattern and colour variations, from drab ones to light yellow striped ones. In most cases these variations are not the result of culling but normal variation found in nature.

Like all dwarf shrimp, they usually grow to 2–3 cm. In a proper aquarium with optimal conditions they can reproduce and live up to 1.5–2 years.
They are native to the islands of Sulawesi in Indonesia.

Malawa shrimp do not need much space and can be kept in containers as small as 20 litres. However, it is difficult to keep a proper balance in such small tanks, so a tank of at least 40 litres is advised, especially for beginners.

The tank must be fully cycled; they cannot survive the cycling period. Like all dwarf shrimp, they are susceptible to ammonia, nitrites and nitrates.

Temperature: they tolerate 21–32 °C, but the optimal range is 24–27 °C. They thrive in warmer temperatures, though room temperature usually suits them. A heater is recommended for the most efficient breeding.

pH: although they come from areas with a high pH, they can also tolerate lower pH. The optimal pH is 7.0–8.5.

Hardness: optimal KH 1–10 and GH 4–15.

RO/DI water remineralised with Salty Shrimp GH/KH+ is recommended; tap water can be used but is not a good option.

Acclimate them carefully and very slowly, as with all invertebrates; 2–3 hours is generally enough. Be careful with chemicals such as copper: crabs, shrimp and crayfish do not tolerate copper-based medications.

Substrate: unlike many other Caridina, Malawa shrimp do not need an active (buffered) substrate and prefer an inert substrate, which does not change water chemistry (pH).

Filtration: sponge filters are the best option because of their surface area. Matten filters are highly recommended for any shrimp tank.

Light: light is not important for the shrimp; adapt it to the needs of the plants in the tank.

Decorations and plants: not necessary, but give them places to hide. Driftwood and plants are excellent for this and provide a lot of surface area for biofilm, which makes up most of their food in nature.

Like most freshwater shrimp, Malawa shrimp are scavengers and omnivores. They are not picky and eat just about any food they find. In a well-established aquarium they can usually find enough food (algae and biofilm) by themselves.

To keep them healthy, supplement with common shrimp foods. They will also eat algae wafers, blanched zucchini, cucumber, lettuce, carrots and spinach, and are good at eating mosquito larvae.

Overfeeding is a sure way to kill shrimp. Feed once a day (or once every 2–3 days in a mature tank). Give rations that last 3–6 hours at most, then remove uneaten food to prevent poor water quality and parasite contamination.

Calcium plays a big role for shrimp.

These shrimp are not shy; they are quite bold and active regardless of the time of day, which makes them a good choice for a peaceful community tank. They are completely harmless, not territorial and prefer large groups. The bigger the colony, the safer they feel and the more confident they act.

The ideal situation is a species tank, but they can be kept with other fish in a community tank if those are chosen with care. Large and/or aggressive fish should be avoided. Suitable tankmates are equally peaceful and share the same water parameters.

Malawa shrimp are compatible with:

  • Shrimp (Cherry shrimp, Snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. Babaulti, Ghost shrimp, Amano shrimp, Blue tiger shrimp, Blue Velvet shrimp, Blue Bolt shrimp, Vampire shrimp, Crystal shrimp, Bamboo shrimp, Cardinal shrimp, Red Nose shrimp, etc.)
  • Freshwater snails (for example Japanese trapdoor snails, Ramshorn snails, Nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, Black Devil snails, Asolene spixi, Rabbit snails, White Wizard snails, etc.)
  • Small and peaceful fish (for example Pygmy corydoras, Otocinclus)

Keep them away from all types of crayfish and crabs. Even small African dwarf frogs will try to catch the shrimp whenever possible.

• Larger shrimp are females; males are smaller.
  • Females carry eggs, so their abdomen is wider and curves down to protect the eggs. Males have thinner abdomens.
  • Females may show a saddle (on the upper body behind the head, where eggs are stored before fertilisation).

They are very easy to breed, with no specific water requirements for the hatchlings. Once they adapt and water parameters suit them, berried females (eggs under the abdomen) appear.

The female keeps the eggs for the whole incubation, which ranges from 4–6 weeks depending on temperature, fanning them regularly with her pleopods. She then releases up to 30 fully developed shrimplets, tiny copies of the adults of no more than 2 mm and fully independent.

If you use hang-on-back or canister filters, cover the intake, as baby shrimp can be pulled in.

Malawa shrimp do not interbreed with other Caridina or Neocaridina species, so there is no risk of hybridising. The only problem is that they can outcompete other shrimp species for food and outbreed them.

In the shrimp hobby they are described as Caridina pareparensis parvidentata. There is no such species: Caridina pareparensis and Caridina parvidentata are two different species. The two are probably very hard to tell apart, so Malawa shrimp received this 'new' name in the aquarium hobby to simplify identification.
